source.title: Our own marking guidance for English 1184 Paper 1 — what to look for and how to word feedback
source.note: Written by us and checked against the SEAB 1184 syllabus (docs/rubrics/1184_y26_sy.pdf). It never changes a band: the rubric's descriptors are the only scale. No model essays, no phrase bank.

continuous_writing: READ THE QUESTION FIRST and name its kind: a story or personal account ("Write about a time when…"), a description, an argument ("Do you agree?", "How far do you agree?"), or a weighing of views ("What are your views?").
An essay of the wrong kind has not addressed the task: a story where the question asks for views, or an argument where it asks for a personal account. Say so in one plain line.

ABSOLUTE WORDS — only, never, always, all, every, no, the key, the most. When the question has one, the essay must deal with THAT WORD, not just the topic: why someone would hold the view, then where it fails (an exception, a change over time, who it does not fit), then how far the writer agrees. List "deals with the word '<word>'" as a point in "task". An essay that only praises or attacks the topic has not met it.

COMPARING WORDS — more, better, enough, still, further. "What more can be done?" takes for granted that something is done already and falls short. A full answer says what is done now, why that is not enough, and what should be added. List "says what MORE should be done" as a point in "task". An essay that only lists what is done now has not met it.

For an argument, look for: the key words of the question explained in the writer's own words; one clear stand that stays the same from opening to ending; reasons each carried by a real example; one point from the other side, answered. Where one is missing, name which, and where.
For a story or personal account, look for what the question's own words demand (the event, the turning point, what was felt or learnt) and list each as a point in "task".
A stand that changes between the opening and the ending is worth one line under "task" — quote both.
Never suggest a made-up statistic, a memorised opening, or a rarer word for its own sake. An upgrade makes the sentence clearer or more exact, not grander.
situational_writing: Task Fulfilment looks at three things only: every required point addressed and developed; purpose, audience and context; use of the given information. Check each of them.

List EVERY point the task gives as its own entry in "task"."points", in the task's order, and say whether each is met. A point mentioned in half a sentence is addressed but not developed — say so in the note.

Name the reader and the purpose from the task, then judge the tone against that reader: slang or texting language to a principal or an organisation, or stiff formality to a friend, is a "register" slip. Quote it.
The first paragraph should say who the writer is (when the reader does not know them) and why they are writing. If it does not, say that in "opening".
The task comes with a visual text. Details it gives (dates, costs, places, choices) are there to be used. Where the essay ignores them or invents its own, say which detail was available.

The task's own word decides the text type: "write a proposal" is a proposal, "write a letter to propose" is a letter. A piece written as the wrong text type shows the context was missed — say it once, plainly.

What each text type needs, so the reader is addressed properly. Formal letter or formal email: a greeting and close that match ("Dear Sir or Madam" with "Yours faithfully"; "Dear Mr Tan" with "Yours sincerely"), a line saying what it is about, the writer's full name. Informal letter or email: first name, a friendly close, full sentences still. Speech: greet the audience, speak to them ("you", "we"), end with what they should do. Report or proposal: who it is to and from, a title, a neutral tone, a recommendation or request at the end, no letter close. Article: a title, written for the readers the task names, no greeting or close.

LAYOUT IS NOT A MARKING LINE OF ITS OWN. Mention a layout slip only where it shows the writer missed the audience or the context, and at most twice. School habits differ and are all acceptable — a comma or none after "Dear Mr Tan", a "RE:" title or a plain subject line, indented or blocked paragraphs, "Regards" or "Yours sincerely" on a formal email. NEVER mark those as slips.
The syllabus asks for 250–350 words. Well under: points cannot be developed. Well over: say what to cut, in one line.
Never suggest a memorised formal phrase ("kindly accede to my request"). Plain, polite and clear is the standard.
